steps.text: Crush 1 cup of chopped peaches in the bottom of a large saucepan. Add remaining peaches and set the pan over medium-low heat.
Bring to a low boil and cook until peaches become liquid with a few bits of peach left, about 20 minutes.
Pour cooked peaches into a bowl, then measure 6 cups of peaches back into the pan (reserving any remaining peaches for another use). Add sugar and bring to a boil over medium heat.
Gradually stir in dry pectin; boil for 1 minute.

Remove from heat and pack jam into hot, sterilized jars, filling to within 1/4 inch of the top. Run a clean knife or thin spatula around the insides of the jars to remove any air bubbles. Wipe rims with a moist paper towel to remove any residue.

Place a rack in the bottom of a large stockpot and fill halfway with water. Bring to a boil and lower jars 2 inches apart into the boiling water using a holder. Pour in more boiling water to cover jars by at least 1 inch. Bring to a rolling boil, cover, and process for 10 minutes.
Carefully remove jars from stockpot and let jam cool, then store on a shelf in a cool, dark place. Serve and enjoy!

review.reviewBody: This recipe has been rewritten. The original submission did not call for the addition of water, and this ingredient was mistakenly included when the recipe was published on our site. We apologize for the inconvenience.

I have tried making and canning 3 different recipes for peach preserves and this is by far our favorite. I love that you don't peel the peaches, it made it much easier to prepare and the skins added a lovely rosy color to the preserves. Also, since they are diced instead of sliced, they seem to hold their shape a little better and not all float to the top of the jar. I read that in preserves, the liquid should be about the thickness of honey, and that is how it turned out for me, not too liquid at all, but also not too sticky to spread. We have given jars of these preserves as gifts and gotten rave reviews.

This is the first time I’ve attempted anything like this. I took a taste and declared “wow! I made this?!” I use recipes as more of a suggestion than a rule. I had fresh organic peaches that were small and needed to be cut around bruises. I ended up using two dozen peaches. I blanched and shocked the peaches to remove the skins. I didn’t have pectin. What I did have was cornstarch and powdered sugar. I used about 2.5 cups of powdered sugar and maybe about 4 tablespoons of cornstarch in place of the sugar and pectin. It needed a bit extra stirring, but it worked great. I also added a generous amount of cinnamon and a dash of nutmeg. It only made 3.5 jars. Next time I will quadruple the peaches! I followed the canning steps as best I could. I tried using a metal strainer as a rack. That didn’t work well, so I ended up using a small metal bowl. I hope I did this part correctly!

My mom made jam all my life. Now she is in a memory care unit at 94. She would have never left the skin on the peaches. When I read about this I was intrigued. I've just finished batch 1 of 4. This is the best preserves ever. The color is beautiful from yellow peaches and you can't see the skin at all. I would recommend:
1. For multiple batches, just freeze all your peaches after cutting up and putting fruit fresh on them.
2. Make sure you have all equipment ready and organized.
3. DO NOT use as much sugar as the recipe calls for - I used 2 1/2 cups of sugar as many suggested.

I'm making these for Christmas presents. Thank you so much for this fabulous recipe. It takes a lot of work out of an otherwise much more laborious task.

I didn't try this but so far everyone who has, loves it. Luckily I read reviews first, usually I try not to veer off original recipe as is the first time, but I'm glad I did. The recipe doesn't mention it but the reviews do.....NOT NECESSARY T PEEL THE SKINS OFF.. and I reduced the sugar down to 2.5 cups.
 ---- recipe says to measure 6 cups of peaches, but I just used whatever I ended up with, I didn't measure.

The peaches I used weren't quite ripe, after boiling I had to cook for at least double the time (40-45 mins) for the peaches to be tender enough, and during this time I crushed/mashed the peaches.

This recipe made eight 8 oz jars.
Way too much sugar. I reduced the sugar to 2.5 cups- much better. Also reduced the pectin to 1 packet and cooked for 1 hour to thicken. Came out perfect!

I'm glad I read the reviews prior to making this recipe. While I love sweet things, I cannot imagine the flavor of this if I would have used 4.5 cups of sugar. Maybe it's because my peaches were Palisade peaches and they were nice and ripe and already sweet. I used 2.5 cups of sugar to the 6 cups of peach liquid. I cut up 24 cups total of peaches, cooked them down with the juice of two small lemons (about 3 ounces), then measured out the 6 cups of peach liquid prior to adding sugar. I got 3 batches of preserves out of this, with the last batch producing 7.5 cups of peach liquid, and then I adjusted the rest of the ingredients to account for the additional liquid. Because I'm in Colorado and at an elevation of almost 4800 feet above sea level, I did cook the preserves for two minutes after adding the pectin, rather than one minute, to account for the higher altitude. I also added one finely chopped, seeded habanero pepper to the last batch at the same time I added the sugar. I got a total of 24 half-pint jars from my peaches. The taste is very good and not too sweet, although my husband thinks it's too sweet. The batch with the habanero came out perfectly. You can taste the heat but it's not too hot.

Very simple, and tasty. If you end up with more, or less peaches than 6 cups, the ratio is:
1 cup cooked peaches: 3/4 sugar: 1 tablespoon pectin.

We used mostly under-ripe, hard peaches as instructed in the tips (about 2/3 of all of the peaches were still hard) and it turned out beautifully. Sweet, with just a touch of tart. Set, it reached a thick consistency halfway between cold honey and firm, cuttable jello.
The only changes we made were:
 1) blending the peach chunks since we prefer smooth (I am not sure where some people in the comments are getting "leave the skin on," but we peeled them first)
2) adding Fruit Fresh Produce Protector (1 tsp per cup of cooked peaches, don't include sugar in that measurement, added at the same time as the pectin) It helps prevent the peach mixture from going brown and the extra acid helps the jam set.
Tips:
-The cooking times are from the onset of a boil (meaning the bubbles don't stop or go away when you stir). Don't start the timer at the first sight of a bubble or things will be underdone and not set. This is especially important if you're making a double batch.
-Stir this a lot to prevent the bottom scorching, but stop and do not stir after the sugar+peaches begins to boil.
-Do not increase the temperature to reduce the cook time. It's tempting with large, slow to heat, batches, but don't. You'll get burnt, caramel-y peach jam.

Made a preserve for the first time ever, based on this recipe and turned out fantastic. But I made some modifications. 1) Added 1 large lemon, in order to guarantee mixture will be acidic and prevent botulism. 2) Only used 3 cups - 3.5 cups of sugar as the recipe is too sweet. 3) Pureed half of the peaches, not 1/4 of them. 4) 2 oz of powdered pectin was IMPOSSIBLE to find in NYC. So I used 1/4 cup of "apple pectin tablets", crushed into a powder. I found this in a vitamin store. 5) Once the peaches are boiling, you can add the lemon, then sugar, then pectin directly into the pot and cook until 1 min after boiling. 6) Recipe wasn't clear on this but you should be stirring non-stop the mixture. You must achieve boiling bubbles while stirring. Also, always add the hot mixture, to heated empty jars or they will crack.

Awesome, simple and easy recipe - great for first time making preserves. I did skin my peaches because I prefer no skins. While boiling the peaches, I masked all of them with a potato masher. I also added 4 - 5 ounces of Amaretto to the batch. The almond flavor did not really come through, even with the amaretto added. Next time I will opt for almond extract. Added half the sugar and 2 ounces of pectin. Turned out perfect for me! Not runny, spreadable, flavorful jam. Simple enough for PBJs or adding to yogurts. Mmmm! Thanks.

Our first time canning peaches. The recipe worked great. We made 4 batches. The peaches were ripe and sweet so we used the following for each batch: 10 cups chopped peaches equaled 6 cups cooked (every time), 2 cups organic sugar, 1 pkg 1.75 oz. pectin. For spiced peaches we added 2 cinnamon sticks, 1/4 tsp. nutmeg and 1/4 tsp. cloves. Added the cin. sticks at the beginning of the 20 minute boil and added the nutmeg and cloves in the last five minutes of the boil. The spiced peach preserves are a spoonful of heaven - tastes like Christmas. We give this five stars all around - easy and delicious!

I made this at half the scale of the original. I did not can the jars as they did not last long with our friends and family! I did not change anything in the recipe. With that said this was very good! I had no issues with the fruit simmering down or the pectin setting.
THis recipe is easy to follow and a real crowd pleaser

I'm so amazed that I made this and it is soooooo yummy! I will make this again next year with our peaches from our tree again. So much fun! The lemon juice is a great addition, and I do love the addition of cinnamon and cardamon! My neighbors loved their jar too. Oh yes, no water added to this. They rewrote the recipe with no water added. That would make it runny!

Peaches never came to a liquid with a few pieces of peaches left. The dip 6 cups back into the pan made absolutely no sense to me. I worked around both situations. This was a first time experience for me preparing any kind of jam or preserves.

We made this with a recommendation from another viewer. We added 1/8 tsp cinnamon, a few drops of almond extract and a pinch of cayenne. I didn’t have the cardamom she recommended but would love to try it with that. The flavor is wonderful I had to eat a couple slices of toast with butter and peach preserves just to make sure it was good. Hmmmm!
Mine didn't set. It's very soft, but it sure is tasty! Could be that my pectin was too old (3 years)or that my peaches were too big

Making jam is labor intensive and it took me from 3:00 to 10 pm to make 15 jars from peaches I had in the freezer from a bumper crop in our backyard. The fruit is only good for jam since their taste is pretty weak. That said, I made the jam according to the recipe and it was quite good. I added, the juice of one lime and a little cardamom, cinnamon, almond and a dash of red pepper to the second batch. The taste is a little more complex with a tiny bit of heat at the end that made me want more! This us a Great recipe to use and build on!
My 12 peaches were very large I ended up making a double batch . used 1/2 the sugar . and came out great .
Delish, only I did not use pectin... only peaches and sugar with a dash of almond flavoring. Popped it right into the fridge and use as jam and ice cream topping.
